text.p: President Ernesto Samper lashed out on Wednesday at the "financial pirates" who he said had contributed to Colombia's economic crisis and were the same people who unleashed the financial disaster in Mexico three years ago.
"This is a serious country with an economy that has been very well managed for many years now. We don't need financial pirates here," Samper said.

He was referring to bankers and financial market speculators who he said had flooded Colombia with "an avalanche" of dollars last year as they moved to take advantage of the country's sky-high interest rates. The influx of foreign currency caused a sharp appreciation of Colombia's peso currency, which hurt exports and slammed the brakes on economic growth.

"There were speculative movements," Samper said of the abrupt and massive increase in dollars that entered Colombia late last year, pushing central bank foreign reserves up to a record high of nearly $10 billion by the end of December.

"This was done by the same people who caused the tequila effect in countries like Mexico and who could cause serious imbalances in other countries. What we're doing is vaccinating ourselves against that effect," he added.

Samper spoke in an interview with the RCN radio network, two days after he took the unusual step of declaring an economic state of emergency to fight what he called a "worrisome" fiscal deficit that was threatening Colombia's long and jealousy guarded record of economic stability.

Measures announced so far as part of the emergency include a tax on foreign debt sold by local companies, a move that analysts say should help stop the inflow of dollars into the economy and undercut the peso.

Samper did not elaborate on the similarities between Colombia's economic problems and those that led to the peso crisis in Mexico at the start of President Ernesto Zedillo's term in December 1994. But like Mexico three years ago, Colombia is saddled with an overvlaued currency and a burgeoning central government deficit.
Samper, who on Tuesday pledged a sharp cut in government spending, said a failure to reduce the deficit would lead to higher inflation, growing unemployment and slower economic growth.
